document.title: Partial Protest and Comments of Dominion Energy Services, Inc. re PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s Reliability Backstop Procurement proposal

pages.text:
1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
) 
) 
ER26-3380-000
 
 
PARTIAL PROTEST AND COMMENTS OF DOMINION ENERGY SERVICES, INC. 
 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf 
of its affiliate, Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia (“Dominion 
Energy”), hereby submits the following generally supportive comments and partial protest with 
respect to PJM’s proposed rules in the above captioned proceeding that would establish a one-time 
procurement for new capacity to address resource adequacy challenges in the PJM Region.2   
Dominion Energy Virginia, a subsidiary of Dominion Energy, Inc., is a public service 
corporation organized under the laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia and a public utility subject 
to regulation by the Commission and does business in the Commonwealth of Virginia and in the 
State of North Carolina. It is a regulated, vertically integrated public utility engaged in the 
generation, transmission, distribution, and sale of electric energy. Dominion Energy Virginia 
furnishes electric service to approximately 2.8 million retail customers in its approximately 30,000 
square miles of certificated service territory covering parts of Virginia and North Carolina. To 
provide that service, Dominion Energy Virginia owns and operates a diverse fleet of nuclear, oil, 
biomass, pumped storage, hydro, coal, solar, wind and natural gas-fired electric generating 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211 (2026). 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000) (July 31, 2026)(“PJM Filing”). Dominion Energy filed 
a “doc-less” intervention in this proceeding on August 4, 2026.

2 
 
capacity of approximately 21,000 megawatts. Dominion Energy Virginia owns 6,800 miles of 
electric transmission lines in Virginia, North Carolina and West Virginia, which is operated by 
PJM. Dominion Energy Virginia joined PJM effective May 1, 2005, after obtaining prior approval 
from the Commission, the Virginia State Corporation Commission, and the North Carolina Utilities 
Commission.3 
I. 
Introduction 
The PJM Filing proposes reforms to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) 
and the Reliability Assurance Agreement to establish a Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) 
that creates a one-time procurement of new, incremental capacity to address ongoing resource 
adequacy challenges in the region that are driven by unprecedented load growth from large load 
in the PJM region.4  While PJM’s proposed RBP is a product of the Critical Issue Fast Past 
(“CIFP”) process, it is one of several feasible solutions that are aligned with the National Energy 
Dominance Council’s (“NEDC”) and the PJM Governors’ statement of principles (“Statement of 
Principles”) and the PJM Board Letter.5   PJM proposes to commence the RBP on September 30, 
2026 to procure new capacity in response to the capacity shortfalls observed in the Reliability 
Pricing Model (“RPM”) Auctions for the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years (“DY”).6 
 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 109 FERC ¶ 61,012 (2004), on reh’g in part, 110 FERC ¶ 61,234 (2005); Ex Parte: 
In the matter concerning the application of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Virginia Power 
for approval of a plan to transfer functional and operational control of certain transmission facilities to a regional 
transmission entity, V.S.C.C. Case No. PUE-2000-00551, Order Granting Approval (Nov. 10, 2004); In the Matter 
of Application of Virginia Electric and Power Company, d/b/a Dominion North Carolina Power, for Authority to 
Transfer Functional Control of Transmission Assets to PJM Interconnection, LLC, N.C.U.C. Docket No. E-22, Sub 
418, Order Approving Transfer Subject to Conditions (Apr. 19, 2005). 
4 Capitalized terms not otherwise defined herein have the meaning as defined in the Tariff, Amended and Restated 
Operating Agreement of PJM (“Operating Agreement”), RAA, and Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement 
(“CTOA”). 
5 Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, National Energy Dominance Council, 2 (Jan. 16, 2026)(available at 
https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm). Board Decisional Letter on Critical Issue 
Fast Path - Large Load Additions, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C, (January 16, 2026)(available at 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2026/20260116-pjm-board-
letter-re-results-of-the-cifp-process-large-load-additions.pdf).   
6 PJM Filing at p. 27.

3 
 
As explained below, Dominion generally supports the RBP as a one-time procurement to 
bring the PJM region to a more stable state of resource adequacy and pave the way for holistic 
market design reforms that will support the infrastructure needed to reliably serve load growth in 
the region.  However, Dominion Energy believes aspects of the PJM Filing’s proposed cost 
allocation for the RBP are unjust and unreasonable in the way that they determine each Electric 
Distributor (“ED”) zone/area’s share of the Final RBP Target.  Dominion Energy respectfully 
requests the Commission approve the PJM Filing subject to PJM submitting a compliance filing 
to adjust the allocation methodology. 
II. 
Comments 
The RBP is not an answer to PJM’s resource adequacy problem but is a necessary stop-gap 
solution to stabilize the region and allow for a more holistic review of the markets.  The PJM 
region must address near-term deficiencies to begin focusing on the long-term solution, which is 
why Dominion Energy supports the RBP.  Ideally, the combination of PJM’s wholesale markets, 
resource adequacy and transmission planning, interconnection processes, and market participant 
obligations work together to reliably and affordably build out the infrastructure necessary to 
support future load growth.  PJM is not there yet, and it may take several years for any holistic 
reforms to have an impact.  For this reason, the RBP presents an opportunity to bring resource 
adequacy up to PJM’s reliability requirement through the procurement of new dispatchable 
generation needed in the region.    However, it is important to recognize that the ability of the RBP 
to attract significant new investment is because it offers long-term certainty required by developers 
that is currently not afforded in the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) design.  Future reforms of 
the capacity and energy markets must address this issue: a 3-year forward auction sending a one-
year price signal can no longer be the sole means to attract the generation needed to meet future

4 
 
load growth.  The bilateral matching process initiated by PJM is a good first step to promoting the 
types of long-term contracting needed to attract new capacity outside the RPM Base Residual 
Auction (“BRA”), but future reforms must examine whether the incentives and obligations for 
Load Serving Entities bringing on new large loads in the region is sufficient to bring the new 
capacity required.7 
III. 
Partial Protest 
A. PJM’s proposed methodology for allocating the Final RBP Target to individual 
ED zone/areas is unjust and unreasonable. 
 
Dominion does not oppose the underlying principle of PJM’s cost allocation approach for 
the RBP.  Recognizing that much of the shortfall experienced in the last two capacity auctions is 
attributable to Large Load adjustments added to the load forecasts, PJM proposes pro-rata 
allocation to ED zone/areas based on their share of forecasted load growth between the 2026/2027 
and 2028/2029 Delivery Years (“MW Load Adjustment Share”).8  However, PJM’s proposed two-
step process fails to recognize that a portion of each ED zone/area’s Incremental Large Load Share 
was covered by the past two capacity auctions.  Instead, PJM would require ED zone/areas seeking 
to fully offset their potential RBP allocation to demonstrate a capacity offset equivalent to their 
entire MW Load Adjustment Share rather than just their Initial RBP Target allocation.9  This leads 
to potential double charging for capacity requirements and is unjust and unreasonable.  
To understand the issue, it is probably best to first consider what should be the appropriate, 
just and reasonable RBP Target allocation and offset methodology and then contrast that with what 
PJM proposes.  Dominion agrees with PJM’s first step in the process whereby the Initial RBP 
 
7 Id. at p.30. 
8 Id. at p. 31. 
9 Id. at p. 32 (“The amount of capacity by which Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW may reduce the Initial RBP 
Target will also be capped at the Load Adjustment for each Electric Distributor zone/area amount of summer 2028 
demand as set forth in the load forecast.”)

5 
 
Target is allocated to each ED zone/area based on their ratio share of the forecasted load growth 
from the 2026/2027 Delivery Year to the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.10  Each ED zone/area then 
knows how much of the RBP UCAP MW they will be responsible for if there is no offsetting 
capacity submitted to PJM.  If an ED zone/area has Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW (“RBP 
Offset”), it should be able to reduce their Initial RBP Target by that amount on a one for one basis.  
For example, if an ED zone/area has an Initial RBP Target allocation of 1000 UCAP MW and 
demonstrates 900 UCAP MW of RBP Offsets, it will have a 100 UCAP MW share of the Final 
RBP Target and this will become its Reliability Backstop Obligation.  If the ED zone/area submits 
enough RBP Offsets to cover its entire Initial RBP Target allocation, then it should not receive a 
Reliability Backstop Obligation or any further cost allocation for the RBP.  No additional allocation 
step should be required. 
PJM does not follow this straightforward approach. Instead of using the Initial RBP Target 
allocation as the amount that can be offset by an ED zone/area, PJM’s proposal requires the ED 
zone/area to offset its MW Load Adjustment Share.  To illustrate, the Croop Affidavit’s example 
shows one ED zone/area fully offsetting its MW Load Adjustment Share (REC) and a second ED 
zone/area partially offsetting its MW Load Adjustment Share (ODEC).11  Since PJM’s proposal is 
anchored to the MW Load Adjustment values for purposes of offset, it requires a second step that 
converts offsetting UCAP MW into their load MW equivalent to recalculate each ED zone/area’s 
final percentage share of the Final RBP Target.12  There are two significant issues with this 
approach. 
 
10 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.3(a). 
11 PJM Filing, Affidavit of Ms. Danielle Croop (“Croop Affidavit”), at p. 12. 
12 Id. at p. 13.

6 
 
First, requiring ED zone/areas to offset their MW Load Adjustment Share fails to recognize 
that the BRA has already procured capacity for a portion of that MW Load Adjustment Share.  
Consider what PJM’s proposal requires at the region-wide level. The Initial RBP Target of 6,831.3 
UCAP MW represents the amount of UCAP MW needed to bring the PJM region back to 
compliance with the RTO Reliability Requirement for the 2028/2029 DY.13  To fully offset the 
need for the RBP under PJM’s proposed allocation methodology, all identified ED zone/areas 
would need to demonstrate 8,492.1 RBP Offsets (UCAP MWs), calculated by converting the 
9,033.2 MW region-wide Load Adjustment MW by the 2028/2029 BRA Forecast Pool 
Requirement of 0.9401. As a result, ED zone/areas are being asked to bring a surplus of 1,660.8 
UCAP MWs—not needed to meet the Reliability Requirement—to ensure they do not receive a 
portion of the Final RBP Target. This surplus capacity represents an equivalent amount of load that 
participated in the 2028/2029 BRA and was covered by cleared capacity, meaning the load will 
pay for those capacity costs during the Delivery Year.  Requiring ED zone/areas to offset their 
entire MW Load Adjustment Share to avoid having an RBP Obligation raises the possibility that 
they will pay for redundant capacity, which is unjust and unreasonable. 
Second, PJM’s proposed method for allocating the Final RBP Target to ED zone/areas 
presents unjust and unreasonable risks of disproportionally benefiting ED zone/areas that have not 
secured capacity by socializing the benefit of Opt-Outs and RBP Offsets procured in one ED 
zone/area to all ED zone/areas. As discussed above, PJM requires ED zone/areas wishing to avoid 
an RBP Obligation to bring RBP Offsets exceeding their allocation of the Initial RBP Target. PJM’s 
proposal calculates the Final RBP Target as the Initial RBP Target minus RBP Offsets and Opt-
Outs on a 1 MW to 1 MW basis. In this calculation, any RBP Offsets brought by an ED zone/area 
 
13 Id. at p. 2.

7 
 
that surpass their allocation of the Initial RBP Target are effectively credited to other ED zone/areas 
because the total pool of Final RBP Target MWs that are re-allocated out to ED zone/areas has 
decreased by more than the offset-providing ED’s portion of the Initial RBP Target. PJM’s proposal 
unjustly transfers the benefits of an RBP Offset to zone/areas that do not take on the cost-
obligations of procuring the RBP Offset MW; a clear violation of cost causation principles. 
Furthermore, the PJM cost allocation framework breaks down when allocating the Final RBP 
Target if at least 6,831.3 MWs of RBP Offsets have been accepted because the Final RBP Target 
will be set to zero. ED zone/areas that did not bring RBP Offsets will still have remaining MW 
Load Adjustment Shares but will not bear any financial consequences for not bringing RBP Offsets 
because their Final RBP Obligation will be 0 MWs.  
B. Subtracting Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW from Initial RBP Target 
allocations is a just and reasonable methodology for determining the final 
procurement target for individual ED zone/areas. 
 
PJM rightfully determines the region-wide Final RBP Target as the Initial RBP Target 
minus Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MWs and UCAP obligation value of loads opting out of the 
RBP.  However, an ED zone/areas share of the Final RBP Target should not be further adjusted 
based on a recalculation of the MW Load Adjustment values.  Simply allowing ED zone/areas to 
offset their RBP Obligation up to their share of the Initial RBP Target satisfies the overarching 
RBP objective of securing a sufficient amount of capacity for PJM to meet, not exceed, its 
Reliability Requirement. It avoids the potential for load to pay twice for capacity and eliminates 
the potential for ED zone/areas that do not bring RBP Offsets to benefit from ED zone/areas that 
do.  If the FERC chooses to accept the PJM proposal it should do so subject to PJM submitting a 
compliance filing that allows ED zone/areas to offset their share of the Initial RBP Target by

8 
 
providing RBP Offset UCAP MW equal to that share and not an amount equivalent to their MW 
Load Adjustment Share. 
Dominion Energy provides the following edits to PJM’s tariff amendments in sections 18.2 
and 18.3 to effectuate the necessary change: 
18.2 Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW 
 
(e) The total quantity of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW verified by the Office of the 
Interconnection and used to decrement the Initial RBP Target total amount allowed for each 
zone/area will be capped at the Load Adjustment for each Electric Distributor zone/area 
share of the Initial RBP Target as calculated in Tariff, Attachment DD, Section 18.3(a) 
amount of summer 2028 demand as set forth in the load forecast. 
 
18.3 Cost Allocation of RBP Charges, Credits, and Shortfall Charges 
 
(a) Cost Allocation to Electric Distributor zone/area 
 
The Office of the Interconnection shall allocate the Initial RBP Target MW to each Electric 
Distributor’s zone/area using that zone/area’s pro-rata share of the difference between the 
forecasted Load Adjustments for the 2026/2027 Delivery Year and the 2028/2029 Delivery 
Year. 
 
The difference between the forecasted Load Adjustments for the 2026/2027 and the 
2028/2029 Delivery Years Initial RBP Target MW allocated to each Electric Distributor’s 
zone/area shall be reduced for the purpose of this calculation to the extent: 
 
(i) 
an Electric Distributor, LSE, Transmission Owner, or other entity provides 
the Office of Interconnection with evidence of Qualifying RBP Offset 
UCAP MW, in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.2 and as 
may be further set forth in the PJM Manuals; or 
 
(ii) 
an Electric Distributor zone/area meets one of the opt-out provisions set 
forth in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.1(d). 
 
The resulting reduced MW, floored at zero, is used to calculate the zone/area’s assigned 
pro-rata share of the Final RBP Target MW. The zone/area’s assigned share of the Final 
RBP Target MW shall remain constant throughout the fixed, 15-year term. 
 
The Office of the Interconnection shall allocate the total RBP Charges, assessed daily, to 
an Electric Distributor’s zone/area on a pro-rata basis using the zone/area’s assigned share 
of the total Final RBP Target MW across all zone/areas.

9 
 
C. The Commission has the authority to direct modification of the Final RPB 
Target Allocation. 
 
PJM has consented to modification of its proposal where such modification is consistent 
with PJM’s overarching objectives.14 This change will not affect those objectives and will in fact 
better align with cost allocation principles and the design of the RBP.  This change will not have 
any adverse effect on other aspects of the design and should not cause any delay. 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
Dominion Energy respectively requests that the Commission grant PJM’s proposed Tariff 
revisions subject to PJM submitting a compliance filing for the reasons discussed above.  
 
Respectfully submitted,
